results.name: partial_last_digit_match
results.description: For sets whose examples do NOT all share a last digit, yes rate among non-example targets sharing a last digit with at least one example minus those sharing none; the model only rewards last-digit matches via full 'ends in d' rules, so observed above null means people use feature-level digit similarity to individual examples more than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: partial_last_digit_match
# description: For sets whose examples do NOT all share a last digit, yes rate among non-example targets sharing a last digit with at least one example minus those sharing none; the model only rewards last-digit matches via full 'ends in d' rules, so observed above null means people use feature-level digit similarity to individual examples more than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)  # (rows, <=4), NaN pad
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    dist = np.abs(ex - t[:, None])
    nearest = np.nanmin(dist, axis=1)
    nonmember = nearest > 0
    ld = np.mod(ex, 10)
    all_same = np.nanmax(ld, axis=1) == np.nanmin(ld, axis=1)
    share = np.any(ld == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    m = nonmember & ~all_same
    a, b = r[m & share], r[m & ~share]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: far_rule_consistent_generalisation
results.description: Yes rate among non-example targets more than 10 from every example that are divisible by the examples' common divisor (gcd >= 2) — i.e. distant targets licensed only by an arithmetic rule; observed above null means people generalise broad arithmetic rules to distant numbers more than the model predicts, below null means less.
results.code:
# name: far_rule_consistent_generalisation
# description: Yes rate among non-example targets more than 10 from every example that are divisible by the examples' common divisor (gcd >= 2) — i.e. distant targets licensed only by an arithmetic rule; observed above null means people generalise broad arithmetic rules to distant numbers more than the model predicts, below null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)  # (rows, <=4), NaN pad
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    dist = np.abs(ex - t[:, None])
    nearest = np.nanmin(dist, axis=1)
    nonmember = nearest > 0
    e = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=0.0).astype(np.int64)
    g = np.gcd.reduce(e, axis=1)
    m = nonmember & (nearest > 10) & (g >= 2) & (np.mod(t.astype(np.int64), np.maximum(g, 1)) == 0)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[m].mean())

results.name: proximity_gradient
results.description: Yes rate among non-example targets within 3 of the nearest example minus among those 20+ away; observed above null means human generalisation falls off with numerical distance more steeply than the model's interval hypotheses predict, below null means less steeply.

results.name: cell_unanimity
results.description: Fraction of (set, target) cells with >=2 responses where all responses agree; observed above null means people are more consistent with each other (more deterministic/extreme yes-probabilities) than the model's graded posterior predicts, below null means more disagreement.

results.name: example_count_tightening
results.description: Yes rate on non-example targets for 1-2-example sets minus for 3-4-example sets; observed above null means people tighten generalisation with more examples more than the tempered model predicts, below null means less.

results.name: decade_boundary_effect
results.description: Among non-example targets 1-9 away from the nearest example, yes rate when the target shares its tens digit (decade) with some example minus when it does not; the model's intervals are decade-blind (~0 expected), so observed above null means people generalise within decades more than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: decade_boundary_effect
# description: Among non-example targets 1-9 away from the nearest example, yes rate when the target shares its tens digit (decade) with some example minus when it does not; the model's intervals are decade-blind (~0 expected), so observed above null means people generalise within decades more than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)  # (rows, <=4), NaN pad
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    dist = np.abs(ex - t[:, None])
    nearest = np.nanmin(dist, axis=1)
    nonmember = nearest > 0
    same_dec = np.any(np.floor(ex / 10) == np.floor(t / 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    m = nonmember & (nearest <= 9)
    a, b = r[m & same_dec], r[m & ~same_dec]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: trial_index_drift
results.description: Pearson correlation between trial_index and the yes response; the model has no session dynamics so predicts ~0 — observed above null means people say yes more as the session goes on, below null means they grow more conservative.

results.name: first_vs_last_example_proximity
results.description: Among non-example targets within 10 of some example in multi-example sets, yes rate when the nearest example is the first shown minus when it is the last shown; the order-invariant model predicts ~0, so observed above null means a primacy effect (first example weighted more), below null a recency effect.
results.code:
# name: first_vs_last_example_proximity
# description: Among non-example targets within 10 of some example in multi-example sets, yes rate when the nearest example is the first shown minus when it is the last shown; the order-invariant model predicts ~0, so observed above null means a primacy effect (first example weighted more), below null a recency effect.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)  # (rows, <=4), NaN pad
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    dist = np.abs(ex - t[:, None])
    nearest = np.nanmin(dist, axis=1)
    nonmember = nearest > 0
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    d = np.where(np.isnan(dist), np.inf, dist)
    idx = np.argmin(d, axis=1)
    m = nonmember & (n >= 2) & (nearest <= 10)
    a, b = r[m & (idx == 0)], r[m & (idx == n - 1)]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())
